correctness.rationale: Marking an s-block in a uniform fixed-k partition gives E[N_s]=binom(n,s)S(n−s,k−1)/S(n,k) and conditional singleton mean μ(n−s,k−1); subtraction proves the normalized covariance exactly. For r≥2, μ(r+t,r)=r q_t/p_t for q_t=[z^t]((e^z−1)/z)^(r−1) and p_t=[z^t]((e^z−1)/z)^r. Positive strictly log-concave reciprocal-factorial coefficients and convolution show q_t strictly log-concave, so p_t/q_t strictly increases and μ decreases with m. This forces strict increase with s. The deterministic identity sum(s−1)N_s=n−k makes the weighted covariances sum zero, forcing opposite endpoint signs; k=2 is handled separately by μ(m,1). Independent exact Stirling-ratio and weighted-identity tests passed for 528 (n,k) pairs through n=35. Conditional box occupancy partitions are uniform because each k-block partition has (q)_k labelings.

broader_coverage.reasoning: Bóna–Mező real-rootedness/mode of no-singleton partitions and Barbour–Gnedin general infinite-occupancy asymptotics do not dominate a fixed-(n,k) finite conditional covariance law. A general joint-moment identity could imply the marked-block expression, but not automatically its all-sizes strict sign transition.

value.rationale: Conditioning on partition richness produces a nontrivial complete sign-order law for singleton–block-size dependence; the possible zero, negative plateau at k=2, and exact occupancy equivalence make a useful finite statistical reference. It requires more than recomputing a known Stirling table.

final_claim: For a uniform partition of n labeled elements conditioned on k blocks, 2≤k≤n−2, Cov(N1,Ns)/E[Ns]=μ(n−s,k−1)−μ(n,k). For k≥3 the normalized covariance strictly increases over feasible sizes and crosses zero once (possibly with a zero), while k=2 has a negative plateau and positive final size. The same law holds for uniform occupancy conditioned on exactly k occupied boxes.
limitations: A general finite joint-moment/covariance theorem for fixed-count Stirling partitions might subsume the conditional expression and its monotonicity.
